extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, patent lawyers, judges, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Legal- and policy-focused criteria for evaluating the constitutionality and procedural scope of PTO reexamination/post-grant review provisions (Sections 6 and 18 of the America Invents Act) and related procedural doctrines. Intended to guide whether expanded administrative review of issued patents is permissible and how it should operate relative to judicial proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Clause balance (promote Progress vs limit patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress’ actions must be directed to striking the balance between encouraging innovation and stifling competition through the grant of patents that do not promote 'the Progress of . . . useful Arts.' This is the standard expressed in the Constitution and it may not be ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Graham v. John Deere Co., Bonito Boats; congressional authority to grant or limit patents is constrained by the constitutional mandate to promote progress. Used to justify reexamination procedures as tools to prevent improvident grants that undermine the constitutional purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents as government-created property subject to public concern and legislative determination
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is not a natural right, but solely a product of positive law; its extent, duration, and validity is a matter that must be determined by the legislative branch. 'The grant of a valid patent is primarily a public concern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Consolidated Fruit Jar Co. and Patlex Corp.; supports premise that Congress may legislate procedures (like reexamination) to correct governmental mistakes in issuing patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and presumption of administrative correctness (35 U.S.C. §282)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory presumption of validity found in 35 U.S.C. Sec. 282 is a reflection of the presumption of administrative correctness by the PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Microsoft v. i4i. But the presumption's force depends on whether the PTO had all material facts before it; if not, the PTO's considered judgment may lose significant force (i4i slip op. at 17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited, ex parte initial examination implies possibility of incomplete record
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are issued after a limited, ex parte process in which the public has no opportunity to participate. The PTO largely only has before it the information provided by the inventor’s attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the PTO may not have all material information at issuance, reexamination provides an opportunity for the PTO to review and correct its own work based on fuller information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination statutory scope and availability (any person, any time on published prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: '[A]ny person at any time may file a request for reexamination by the [PTO] of any claim of a patent on the basis of any prior art' that was published. (35 U.S.C. Sec. 302).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexamination may confirm patentable claims or cancel unpatentable claims; the process is intended to increase the reliability of the PTO’s action by reexamining patents thought 'doubtful.' Cites In re Etter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct grounds and evidentiary scope: inter partes reexamination vs post-grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: A key distinction between the post-grant review procedures and the inter partes reexamination procedures is the grounds and evidence that can be considered: inter partes (as with current law) is limited to whether a patent is invalid for failing to meet novelty and non-obviousness based on patents or printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 6 creates post-grant review (one-year window) that expands the grounds available for challenge beyond the traditional inter partes limits; discussion highlights the difference in permissible theories and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards of proof between courts and PTO/regulatory proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: In litigation a defendant must establish invalidity by the higher standard of clear and convincing evidence; reexamination by the PTO proceeds under different (generally lower) standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why a patent may be upheld in court yet subsequently rejected by the PTO during reexamination; cites Ethicon v. Quigg and Translogic examples to illustrate differing outcomes under different standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination purpose: corrective governmental function, not a 'taking'
rubrics_metrics.description: The reexamination statute’s purpose is to correct errors made by the government, to remedy defective governmental (not private) action, and if need be to remove patents that should never have been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Patlex Corp.; framing reexamination as remedying governmental mistakes under Congress’s Article I authority and thus not an unconstitutional taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: No constitutional bar from Article III/Seventh Amendment to administrative reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no conflict between Section 6 and other parts of the Constitution such as Article III and the Seventh Amendment; investment of regulatory/validity functions in an administrative agency is consistent with precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases rejecting claims that PTO reexamination 'overrules' Article III court determinations (In re Swanson, Patlex, Joy Technologies). Emphasizes differing proceedings and evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior judicial finding of 'not invalid' is not binding on subsequent PTO reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts do not find patents 'valid,' only that the patent challenger did not carry the burden of establishing invalidity in the particular case before the court under 35 U.S.C. 282. A prior holding of validity is not necessarily inconsistent with a subsequent holding of invalidity and is not binding on subsequent litigation or PTO reexaminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ethicon and In re Swanson; explains why reexamination after a court decision does not violate separation of powers or final-judgment principles because the proceedings use different standards and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamination does not 'undo' a final court judgment; Rule 60(b) remains the mechanism for relief from judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO has no authority to disturb a final judgment of a court, and nothing in the proposed Act would change that. It remains within the discretion of the district court to determine whether relief from a final judgment was appropriate under Rule 60(b) based on changed circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Amado v. Microsoft; clarifies interplay between administrative invalidation and judicial finality; administrative invalidation does not automatically vacate prior court judgments absent appropriate judicial procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authority to target subsets of patents for closer review (rational basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is well within its authority to determine that a particular subset of patents warrant closer administrative review than other patents due to their history and development (e.g., business-method patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues business-method patents were novel and proliferated post-State Street; given confusion and paucity of prior art, Congress may rationally focus resources (Section 18) to ensure adequate vigor in PTO decisions. Cites Bilski, eBay concurrence noting 'suspect validity' of some business-method patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Second bite at the apple' rebuttal—distinct forums and standards justify multiple proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a more robust reexamination procedure does not create a second bite at the apple because patents are continuously subject to challenge in different proceedings with different standards; reexamination answers whether the PTO made a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses analogy to criminal/acquittal vs civil liability; cites Translogic where district court upheld patent but PTO later found it invalid in reexamination. Section 18 merely allows broader invalidity arguments to PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting review to asserted patents as resource-allocation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting the review of existing business-method patents to those that have actually been asserted in court (or threatened to be asserted) serves to limit the burden on the PTO and to focus limited resources on patents more detrimental to the economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to limiting challenges to land claims to competing users; presented as a constitutionally permissible policy judgment about prioritizing PTO workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay of litigation pending reexamination: district court discretion and appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: A party that initiates a PTO reexamination may also seek a stay of ongoing litigation pending reexamination from the court where the litigation is pending; it is the court, not the PTO, that decides whether or not to grant a stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 18(c) provides factors for the district court to consider (similar to existing practice); immediate appellate review of stay decisions is provided to prevent abuse. Cites Medichem v. Rolabo and several district-court decisions applying stay factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping/threshold to obtain reexamination (higher threshold under Sections 6/18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 6 and 18 include higher-threshold gatekeeping functions required to obtain reexamination in the first place, distinguishing the proposed procedures from prior reexaminations limited solely to new prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defends expansion of available grounds as constitutionally insignificant; emphasizes that reexamination availability is subject to statutory thresholds and procedural safeguards.
